explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The verse says the man who isolates himself "…pursues selfish desires…" and the whole picture is one guy, one wish list. Nobody else gets a vote in that house. I spent years in a drawer with nobody to ask what I wanted, and I'm telling you, it did NOT make me wiser.

Close, but a man who has cut himself off from everybody isn't hanging around long enough to chase his neighbor's wishes. The verse says he "…pursues selfish desires…" Selfish means the desires belong to himself. His neighbor isn't even getting a wave over the fence.

I see why you'd go there, but the king doesn't show up in this verse at all. It says the man who isolates himself "…pursues selfish desires…" so the wishes are his own. He's not out there serving anybody. He's running his own little show with an audience of one.

Not this time, baker. The verse says the opposite: he "…rebels against all sound judgment." He isn't going along with it, he's pushing against ALL of it. Cut yourself off from everybody and nobody's left to tell you when you're off course.

That's right. Proverbs 18:1 says the man who isolates himself "…rebels against all sound judgment." Going along with it would be the other direction entirely. I think when nobody's around to say "hey, maybe not," that rebelling gets real easy.

You got it, baker. The fool "…does not delight in understanding, but only in airing his opinions." Understanding means taking something in, and he's all about sending his own stuff out. He's a mixer with no bowl, just spinning.
I get it, money is a classic fool move in other spots. But this verse isn't talking about cash. It says he delights "…only in airing his opinions." His treasure is whatever he's about to say next.
Sleeping all day isn't in this verse. The fool "…does not delight in understanding, but only in airing his opinions." The delight here is opinions, not naps. I bet he's got a lot to say.
That's the one, baker. "With a wicked man comes contempt as well…" Notice the "as well." The wicked man doesn't show up alone, he drags something along with him.

Honor sounds like a nice thing to come along with somebody, but it isn't in this verse. It says "With a wicked man comes contempt as well…" Honor shows up in a different spot, at the end of verse 12, where humility is involved.

Peace would be a lovely guest, but it didn't get the invitation here. The verse says "With a wicked man comes contempt as well, and shame is accompanied by disgrace." The wicked man's entourage is not a calm bunch.

Yes, baker. The verse says "the fountain of wisdom is a bubbling brook." So the verse sets two pictures of water side by side: a man's words as deep waters, and wisdom as a bubbling brook. I think a brook that keeps bubbling is a nice picture of wisdom that doesn't run dry.
Quarrels do come up with the fool, but in verse 6, not here. In verse 4 the brook belongs to "the fountain of wisdom…" Wisdom's the one bubbling along, not the fool.

explanations.answer: The wealth of a rich man
explanations.explanation: Wealth doesn't get a turn until verse 11. In verse 4, the bubbling brook is "the fountain of wisdom…" Nobody's counting money by this stream.

True, baker. The verse says showing partiality to the wicked is not good, "…nor is depriving the innocent of justice." So it names both as not good. One is showing partiality to the wicked, and the other is depriving the innocent of justice.

This one's True, friend. The verse says "Showing partiality to the wicked is not good, nor is depriving the innocent of justice." That "nor" brings in the second thing. Both are called out in the same line.
There it is. "A fool’s lips bring him strife…" He opens his mouth and trouble walks right in. I think we all know somebody who could've skipped a whole week of drama by just not replying.
Honor is a good word, but it belongs to the humble in verse 12. This verse says "A fool’s lips bring him strife…" The lips are working overtime and honor isn't what they're earning.
Rest isn't the word in this verse. It says "A fool’s lips bring him strife, and his mouth invites a beating." Strife is what the lips bring him. I'd pick a nap over that any day.
True, baker. "A fool’s mouth is his ruin, and his lips are a snare to his soul." A snare is a trap. The verse puts that trap on his own lips. That's a lot of trouble for one pair of lips.
It's True, friend. Verse 7 says "A fool’s mouth is his ruin, and his lips are a snare to his soul." The verse calls his own lips the snare. So the trap is right there on his face.
Right. The gossip's words "…go down into the inmost being." I think that's why they stick. A morsel goes down, and then it stays with you.
Gossip does get around, but that's not what this verse says. It says the words are like choice morsels that "…go down into the inmost being." The verse is going inward, not outward.
The city gate isn't in this verse. The morsels "…go down into the inmost being." Down, friend, not up. They land deep inside the one listening.

That's right, baker. The man slothful in his work is "…brother to him who destroys." Sitting on the job and tearing things down are called family. A lazy man might not swing the hammer, but the verse still hands him the family name.

Builds isn't the word the verse uses. It says "Whoever is slothful in his work is brother to him who destroys." The slothful worker is compared to the one who destroys. That's a strong comparison, friend.
Planting isn't the word here. The verse says the slothful man is "…brother to him who destroys." The comparison is to the destroyer. That's a strong line, friend.

explanations.answer: Run to it and are safe
explanations.explanation: You got it. "the righteous run to it and are safe." They run, friend, no strolling and no browsing. And the ones who run to it are the ones who end up safe.
Standing outside isn't what the verse says. It says "the righteous run to it and are safe." Running is the word the verse gives them. And safe is where they end up.
No swords in this verse. It says "the righteous run to it and are safe." Guarding isn't mentioned. The verse has them running to the tower.

Yes, baker. The rich man's wealth is "…like a high wall in his imagination." The wall is real to him, but the verse puts it in his head. Compare that to verse 10, where the tower is the name of the LORD.
No king, no palace in this verse. The rich man's wealth "…is like a high wall in his imagination." It's his own wall, and it's up in his head.
The verse doesn't set the wall at any gate. It says the wealth is "…like a high wall in his imagination." Imagination, friend. That's where the wall stands.
Right, baker. "Before his downfall a man’s heart is proud…" Pride shows up first and the fall comes after. Humility is the other direction: it "…comes before honor." Two paths in one verse.
Fear is a reasonable guess, but the verse names something else. "Before his downfall a man’s heart is proud…" Proud is the word the verse uses, friend. Then comes the downfall.
Quiet is a nice thought, but that's not the word. The verse says "Before his downfall a man’s heart is proud…" Proud is the word, friend. Humility is on the other half of the line.
That's it, baker. "…humility comes before honor." Pride goes in front of a fall, and humility goes in front of honor. Same verse, two roads. I'll gladly take the second line.
Wealth is the topic one verse earlier, but it's not the word here. The verse says "…humility comes before honor." Humility is the one the verse puts before honor, friend.
Strength is a fair guess, but it's not the word. The verse says "…humility comes before honor." Pride sits on the other side with the downfall.

True, baker. "He who answers a matter before he hears it—this is folly and disgrace to him." Answering first and listening later gets a double label. It's both folly and disgrace. Hear first, then answer.
It's True, friend. The verse says the one who answers before he hears the matter is in "…folly and disgrace to him." That's the full tag. Listening first is the fix.

Not quite, baker. The first half is right, since "The spirit of a man can endure his sickness…" But the second half asks "…who can survive a broken spirit?" That's a question with a heavy answer, and it's not easy. I think this line is tender, and it's okay to treat it that way.

That's right. The verse says a man's spirit can endure sickness, then asks, "…who can survive a broken spirit?" So it's not called easy at all. I think this one hurts a little, and it's good to slow down for it.

Yes, baker. "The heart of the discerning acquires knowledge, and the ear of the wise seeks it out." Seeks it out is the key. Wise folks go on a hunt, they don't wait for it to knock. The discerning and the wise are on the same job.

explanations.answer: They wait for it to arrive
explanations.explanation: Waiting by the door is a nice thought, but the verse has them seeking. The ear of the wise "…seeks it out." Seeking is the word the verse uses, friend.

This verse doesn't say anything about hiding. The heart of the discerning "…acquires knowledge, and the ear of the wise seeks it out." It's all about getting it, friend. Going after it, picking it up.

True, baker. "A man’s gift opens doors for him, and brings him before great men." Both halves are in the verse. The gift opens the door, and then it brings the man before great men. That's a lot of work for one gift.
It's True, friend. Verse 16 says a man's gift "…opens doors for him, and brings him before great men." That second part is right there in the text. The gift does the walking for him.
That's it, baker. "The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him." It says seems, friend. The other side comes with questions, and the first story gets tested.

explanations.answer: The judge hands down his ruling
explanations.explanation: No judge is mentioned in this verse. The first one "…seems right until another comes and cross-examines him." The turn comes when the second person shows up with questions.

explanations.answer: The whole crowd takes his side
explanations.explanation: A crowd backing him sounds like it would help him, but it's not in the verse. He "…seems right until another comes and cross-examines him." The second side arrives, and the story gets tested. Seems is the word to watch.

Right. "Casting the lot ends quarrels and separates strong opponents." It does two jobs in one line. The fight ends, and the two strong sides get pulled apart. That's a handy thing to have in a quarrel.
Naming a king isn't in this verse. Casting the lot "…ends quarrels and separates strong opponents." The job here is settling a fight.

Land sounds like a big prize, but this verse isn't about a prize. It says casting the lot "…ends quarrels and separates strong opponents." It's about strong opponents being separated and the quarrel ending. I'd rather read that than referee it.

Not this time, baker. The verse says the opposite: "An offended brother is harder to win than a fortified city…" So it's the harder one. A fortified city has walls, and a hurt brother can be even tougher.
That's right. "An offended brother is harder to win than a fortified city…" Harder, not easier, friend. And the verse adds that disputes are "…like the bars of a castle." Walls and bars in one verse.

True, baker. "From the fruit of his mouth a man’s belly is filled…" Words are talked about like a crop. What you speak is what you end up eating. That's a good reason to watch what comes off the lips.
It's True, friend. Verse 20 says "From the fruit of his mouth a man’s belly is filled; with the harvest from his lips he is satisfied." So the mouth is a field, and the man eats from it.
Yes, baker. "Life and death are in the power of the tongue…" Both are in there, life and death. That's a lot of weight for something so small. And the verse puts it on the tongue.

Wealth is a fair guess, since money shows up in this chapter, but it's not the word here. The verse says "Life and death are in the power of the tongue…" Life and death, friend, riding on one little tongue. I'd trust myself with dough before I'd trust myself with that.
Honor shows up with humility back in verse 12, but not in this verse. Here it's "Life and death are in the power of the tongue…" Death is the other half, friend.

True, baker, because verse 21 says "…those who love it will eat its fruit." That ties right back to verse 20, with the same crop picture. Love the tongue, and you eat what it grows, so plant carefully.
It's True, friend. Verse 21 says "…those who love it will eat its fruit." It picks up the harvest from the verse before. What the tongue grows ends up on the lover's plate.

Yes, baker, the verse puts both in one line: "He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD." The extra blessing is favor from the LORD. That makes two blessings in one verse.
A seat among the elders isn't in this verse. It says he "…finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD." The extra is favor from the LORD.
A dowry isn't mentioned at all. The verse says the man who finds a wife "…finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD." What he gets is favor, friend.

That's right. "The poor man pleads for mercy, but the rich man answers harshly." The verse sets the two side by side. One pleads for mercy, and the other answers harshly. I think this one stings a little.
Gently would be a kind way to answer, but that's not the word. The verse says "The poor man pleads for mercy, but the rich man answers harshly." The "but" is the turn. The rich man's answer is harsh.
A generous answer would be good to hear, but the verse doesn't say that. The poor man pleads for mercy, "…but the rich man answers harshly." That "but" tells you which way the rich man goes.

explanations.answer: One friend who stays closer than a brother
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker, the verse says "A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who stays closer than a brother." It puts one true friend up against a whole crowd. I'd take that one friend.

explanations.answer: A big crowd of loyal neighbors
explanations.explanation: A bigger crowd doesn't help, friend, since the verse already starts with a man of many companions. It says he "…may come to ruin, but there is a friend who stays closer than a brother." The answer is one friend.

explanations.answer: A house full of hired servants
explanations.explanation: Hired servants aren't in this verse. The man of many companions "…may come to ruin, but there is a friend who stays closer than a brother." It's about one friend, friend.
